name: Face-lifting nose pins Tagliacozzi arm-flap rhinoplasty

card.summary: A 16th-century surgical method, published in 1597 by Gaspare Tagliacozzi, that rebuilt a lost or damaged nose with skin grown from the patient's own upper arm.
card.aka: Italian method of rhinoplasty; Tagliacozzi flap; arm-flap rhinoplasty
card.note: A historical technique that required months with the arm immobilized; skin often detached.

quick.overview:
Arm-flap rhinoplasty is the technique described in 1597 by the Bologna surgeon Gaspare Tagliacozzi for rebuilding a nose that had been lost, often to injury. A flap of skin raised from the arm was attached to the nose area and later shaped into a new one.

Its appearance payoff was restoring a facial feature and a more typical look. It is a landmark in the history of plastic surgery and a direct ancestor of modern nasal reconstruction with pedicled flaps.
quick.how: The patient's arm stayed fixed to the face while the flap took, followed by division and shaping of the nose over a period of weeks. The approach is historical and is not a procedure people undertake today.
quick.risks: Contemporary critics and later writers noted that the arm had to be immobilized for many months and that the skin often detached. The method declined across Europe in the 17th century.

lead: Gaspare (Gasparo) Tagliacozzi (1545-1599) was a surgeon and professor at the University of Bologna. His 1597 book De Curtorum Chirurgia per Insitionem described in detail nasal reconstruction methods that the Branca and Vianeo families of Sicily had long practiced empirically.[1]

The method used a flap of skin from the arm, attached to the nose; the arm had to stay immobilized for many months, and the skin often detached, which critics such as Gabriele Fallopio raised.[1] A pedicle flap from the biceps region was attached for about three weeks and the graft shaped into a nose roughly two weeks later.[2]

The aim was reconstructive: to restore a lost nose and a normal-looking face. Tagliacozzi's book is often cited with the line that surgeons restore, rebuild and make whole parts that nature gave but fortune took away.[1]

chain: Skin flap raised from the arm
Attached to the nose site and later divided
angle.text: The technique rebuilt a missing nose from the patient's own skin, restoring a central facial feature. It is documented as an early form of plastic surgery.

infobox: Branca family (Catania, c. 1400) and Vianeo/Boiano brothers (Calabria, 16th c.)[1]
Rediscovered 1800 by Karl Ferdinand von Graefe[1]

paras: Gustavo Branca and his son Antonio in Catania around 1400 are considered the inventors of the Italian method, and the Boiano (Vianeo) brothers practiced it in Calabria in the 16th century.[1] The Sushruta Samhita, which describes rebuilding a nose with a cheek flap, was translated into Arabic in the 8th century, and it has been suggested that such methods may have reached Italy.[1][2] The development of the Italian method has been linked to the popularity of rapier duelling in the 15th to 17th centuries.[1]
Tagliacozzi studied medicine at Bologna from 1565, later became professor of surgery and then anatomy, and from 1568 practiced at the Hospital of Death.[1]

The 1597 book illustrated a nose reattached using a biceps pedicle flap, with the graft detached after about three weeks and shaped roughly two weeks later.[2] Its use declined across Europe in the 17th century, later writers including Fortunio Liceti (1616) and Henricus Moinichen (1691) described it, and it was rediscovered in 1800 by Karl Ferdinand von Graefe and remained in use into the early 20th century.[1]
Compared with the Indian method of a cheek or forehead flap, the Italian method avoided facial scarring at the cost of long immobilization.[2]
No studies found of this historical technique in the modern clinical-trial sense; knowledge of it comes from surgical history.

timeline.event: Gustavo and Antonio Branca practice nasal reconstruction in Catania.[1]
Tagliacozzi publishes De Curtorum Chirurgia per Insitionem.[1]
Karl Ferdinand von Graefe rediscovers the method.[1]
